Adult black sea bass (Centropristis striata) are known to achieve a maximum recorded total length of 66 cm [Li = 66 cm], a size that places them among the larger serranids inhabiting the western Atlantic shelf. During laboratory rearing trials conducted at a stable water temperature of 23.6 °C [T = 23.6 °C], newly hatched yolk-sac larvae emerged from the chorion after an incubation period of only 5.5 days [ab = 5.5 days]. The mass of these prolarvae at the moment of eclosion was measured at 0.000449 grams [Wwb = 0.000449 grams], reflecting the modest dimensions of the pelagic egg from which they hatched, which had a mean diameter of 0.95 mm. This initial wet weight is consistent with values reported for other temperate serranids that produce small, buoyant eggs. The brief embryonic phase and the minimal larval mass at hatching underscore a life-history strategy that prioritizes rapid progression through the vulnerable early planktonic stages, a pattern frequently observed in species that spawn over the continental shelf during the warm months.

The transition to sexual maturity in black sea bass is marked by both a characteristic body length and a corresponding somatic mass. Field surveys indicate that puberty is attained at a total length of 19.1 cm [Lp = 19.1 cm], a size typically reached during the first or second year of life depending on local thermal conditions. The wet weight of individuals at this pubertal milestone has been calculated at approximately 90 grams [Wwp = approximately 90 grams] using length-weight relationships derived from regional stock assessments. This relatively modest size at maturity is typical of protogynous hermaphrodites within the genus Centropristis, where individuals initially mature as females before transitioning to males at larger sizes. The energetic investment in early reproduction is balanced against continued somatic growth, which eventually leads to the much larger asymptotic size exhibited by fully grown adults.

Reproductive output in black sea bass has been characterized through detailed analysis of spawning events under controlled aquarium conditions. At a constant temperature of 23.6 °C [T = 23.6 °C], individual females produced an average of approximately 2,877 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 2,877 eggs per day] during the peak of the spawning season, a rate sustained over the multiple days of a single spawning event. This daily fecundity, extrapolated across the entire breeding period, translates into a substantial annual reproductive effort that is typical of batch-spawning teleosts. The high fecundity per event is partially offset by the small size and high mortality rates experienced by the pelagic eggs and early larvae. These observations were made in specimens maintained at the aforementioned thermal regime, which closely approximates the average water temperatures encountered during the summer spawning season along the mid-Atlantic Bight.

The maximum longevity documented for black sea bass in wild populations is 20 years [am = 20 years], a lifespan that places this species among the longer-lived serranids, a pattern partly attributable to its protogynous sexual system and the relatively stable thermal conditions of its continental shelf habitat, with average annual temperatures near 23.6 °C [T = 23.6 °C]. This extended lifespan allows multiple reproductive seasons and a complex social structure within local aggregations. Older, larger individuals, which are typically male following the sex change, often dominate spawning sites and contribute disproportionately to the next generation. The relationship between body length and wet weight reveals that the largest females, approaching the ultimate total length, achieve a corresponding ultimate wet weight of 3,903 grams (3903 grams) [Wwi = 3903 grams]. This asymptotic mass is consistent with the allometric scaling exponent of 3.04 derived from regional morphometric analyses.

Comparative life-history analyses within the Serranidae family highlight the intermediate position of black sea bass along the fast-slow continuum of life-history strategies. The species exhibits a relatively rapid juvenile growth rate, enabling it to reach the pubertal length of 19.1 cm [Lp = 19.1 cm] and its associated wet weight of 90 grams [Wwp = 90 grams] within a short time frame, yet it also demonstrates a considerable capacity for continued expansion toward the ultimate length of 66 cm [Li = 66 cm]. This growth pattern is influenced by seasonal temperature cycles, with the highest feeding and growth rates occurring during the summer months when coastal waters are warm. The high daily reproductive rate observed at 23.6 °C [T = 23.6 °C] reflects an adaptive response to a relatively short spawning window. Understanding these life-history parameters is critical for fisheries management, as they inform models of population resilience and sustainable harvest levels for this economically valuable species.
